articles.title: Debating Victor Serge
articles.author: Mitchell Abidor
articles.content_excerpt: When I began writing Victor Serge: Unruly Revolutionary , I expected to write a biography in keeping with the image common on the left of Serge as an uncompromising enemy of Stalinism who never fell into anti-communism and fought all his life for revolutionary socialism. This is what we find in the many writings of Richard Greeman, who single-handedly rescued Serge from oblivion by translating his novels and tirelessly writing about him. In fact, my biography began as a collaboration between me and Richard, one we abandoned due to differences in interpretation. Suzi Weissman presents that image as well in her biography of Serge, The Course Is Set on Hope . A fuller account of this Serge was what I thought I was going to write. articles.title: Flock Off: How Westland DSA Members Pushed Flock Cameras Out of Their City
articles.author: Detroit DSA
articles.content_excerpt: By filling city council meetings, educating the public on mass surveillance, and cooperating with like-minded allies, DSA members in Westland shot down a Flock contract renewal. By Dave N. and Kathy E. In July 2024 the city of Westland signed up for a trial run with Flock Safety that would last until August 2026. Flock’s cameras are Automated License Plate Readers (ALPR) that mark the date, time, and location where a vehicle passes. Flock claims that its technology does not scan human faces, but its cameras are able to fingerprint cars based on minute details like rust or bumper stickers. The technology is similar to that used in facial recognition software. articles.author: Red Fault -- Austin DSA
articles.content_excerpt: By Asanti M. The conversation surrounding healthcare access is more than an abstraction of cost and risk, it’s life and death, and people are dying. I know because I’ve pronounced them. I know because I’ve cleaned their lifeless bodies. The burdens of the ailing are only compounded by the general disservice of our institutional frameworks. The nebulous jargon tossed around boardrooms and between pundits materializes in the financial reality that confronts the humanity of the unfortunate and the ailing. articles.title: Texas Wasn’t Always a Right-Wing Evangelical Powerhouse
articles.author: David Griscom
articles.content_excerpt: There’s a common view of religious history that holds that the further back you go, the stronger the smell of brimstone and the more conservative the beliefs. It isn’t true, and it obscures how much the human hand makes the world, including our ideas of the sacred. Joseph L. Locke’s new book One State Under God: A History of Religion in Texas is an important reminder that the conservative evangelical Christianity that dominates Texas, and through it has consolidated its influence over the country, was not a natural outgrowth of Christianity itself, but a product of historical developments. Texas today is at the forefront of the campaign to tear down the wall between church and state. articles.title: Frances Stonor Saunders Exposed the Cultural Cold War
articles.author: Joel Whitney
articles.content_excerpt: With her landmark 1999 debut, Who Paid the Piper? The CIA and the Cultural Cold War , Frances Stonor Saunders “single-handedly established a new branch of sub-history,” as novelist Ian McEwan observed. The book won many accolades, though sympathizers of Western anti-communism clamored to downplay its revelations: that between 1950 and 1967, intelligence agencies partnered in a covert front, launched by the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), to manipulate Cold War intellectuals in a program whose basis was propaganda and censorship. articles.title: Is Trump Crashing the Dollar Empire?
articles.author: Mona Ali
articles.content_excerpt: With more than half of global trade conducted in dollars, the United States is still the world’s largest economy as well as its dominant military and political power. But Donald Trump, in his second presidential term, has put both these facts at unprecedented risk, using America’s global position for political gain and personal enrichment all while undermining the pillars of the nation’s financial dominance, such as the rule of law and the security of global trade flows. Yet according to economist Mona Ali, little of this behavior is truly new. The global financial system is, at its core, a political system, though Trump and his advisers are admittedly wielding this system more carelessly than any administration has in a generation. articles.title: Narratives of Imperfection: Revisiting Harper Lee’s To Kill a Mockingbird (1960) and Go Set a Watchman (2015)
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content_excerpt: by Travis Covitz This month, I re-read To Kill A Mockingbird by Harper Lee for the first time since my freshman year of high school (which overlapped with the first wave of Black Lives Matter uprisings). Mockingbird was written by Lee (a Southern white woman) in the early 1960s; it follows the girlhood of Jean Louise “Scout” Finch, who is white and the daughter of a lawyer, in Depression-era Alabama. A major plot point of the book is Scout’s father, Atticus Finch, defending a local Black man who has been charged with rape of a white woman. Atticus is posed as a noble white hero in contrast with the ‘backwards’ racists in the countryside. articles.title: Social Democracy Won the Century and Lost the Future
articles.author: Bhaskar Sunkara
articles.content_excerpt: On Sunday, Sweden’s Social Democratic Party (SAP) emerged as the largest party in an election that will be remembered for all the wrong reasons. Magdalena Andersson is poised to return as prime minister, with her four-party bloc holding a one-seat majority in a 349-seat Riksdag. The SAP won just 28 percent of the vote, its worst showing in more than 110 years. This is what victory looks like today for the most electorally successful left-of-center party in history. The SAP went from pioneering social democratic governance, ruling almost uninterruptedly for nearly half a century, and even debating the transfer of large firms to worker ownership to serving as a fading bulwark against the far right, with little more than a quarter of the electorate behind it. articles.title: Southern Gothic Films Take On the Horrors of the Past
articles.author: Eileen Jones
articles.content_excerpt: One of the films featured in the Criterion Channel’s “Southern Gothic” series is Baby Doll (1956). It’s based on Tennessee Williams’s one-act plays 27 Wagons Full of Cotton and The Unsatisfactory Supper , which Williams adapted for the screen in collaboration with the most famous interpreter of his work, director Elia Kazan. It begins with the lurid, sexed-up horns of Kenyon Hopkins’s score vamping as if in accompaniment to a strip show as we approach a grimly dilapidated Mississippi plantation house with grimy pillars like the post–Civil War plantation in Gone with the Wind . And there we have in a single film moment a perfect summation of the Southern Gothic.
